questions.q: What evidence confirms the missing-index hypothesis for the slow list view?
options: The query plan shows a full table scan of 2.1 million rows to return a few hundred matches, with no index on the filtered field
The list view's filter condition changed last week
The field it filters on was recently deleted from the table
Instance Health shows no change in list load time at all
questions.explain: A query plan showing a table scan instead of an index seek, on exactly the field the filter depends on, is direct confirmation of a missing index.

questions.q: What is the actual performance problem inside the original ChecklistUtils.getApprovalThresholds function?
options: It runs a brand-new GlideRecord query against u_store_config inside a loop, once per checklist item
It never queries the database at all
It queries a table that doesn't exist
It only runs once per approval batch regardless of batch size
questions.explain: This is a query-in-a-loop (N+1) pattern: one round trip to the store config table for every item in the batch, instead of one query total.

questions.q: What does the fixed version of getApprovalThresholds do differently?
options: It runs the GlideRecord query exactly once and builds a lookup map that the loop reads from
It removes the loop entirely and returns no thresholds
It runs the same query twice instead of once
It queries a different, unrelated table
questions.explain: Moving the query outside the loop and reading from a lookup map produces the same result with one query instead of N.

questions.q: Why did the Nightly Rollup and Morning Reminder scheduled jobs cause a platform-wide slowdown only after growth to 500 stores?
options: Both jobs draw from the same semaphore pool, which only saturates once the 7 AM submission spike from 500 stores is added on top
The jobs were only installed after 500 stores went live
Scheduled jobs always slow down an instance regardless of load
The jobs stopped running once store count passed 50
questions.explain: At 50 stores the shared semaphore pool never saturated; at 500 stores, the jobs plus the submission spike saturate it, forcing other transactions to queue.

questions.q: Why does this lesson confirm all three causes independently rather than stopping after the first one found?
options: Because fixing only one of the three would leave real, reported symptoms unexplained, since each cause explains a different part of the problem
Because only one of the three hypotheses turned out to be real
Because the index, the script, and the scheduled jobs are actually the same underlying bug
Because confirming more than one cause is never useful in a real investigation
questions.explain: The index fixes the list view, the script fixes the flows, and the scheduled jobs fix the 7 AM slowdown -- each is a genuinely separate, compounding cause.
